MIT scientists develop solar panel towers that create 20x the energy output of a flat panel layout per square unit of floor/ground space but, at a higher materials cost.

FTFY

So what does it do? I can see how putting 20 panels in a vertical fashion and had it track the sun would have more output than a stationary panel with the same footprint. Is that seriously what they are reporting on?

First, I want say I find it amusing that the study they are talking about was published in 2012.

The study mostly talks about how their tower (the ones in the thumbnail) generates 2x to 20x the an equivalent base area flat panel in absence of sun tracking. The reason that the tower can achieve higher improvement was due re-absorption of light reflected within the 3D structure. However, the 20x increasing they are stating is for when the solar panels are moved away from the equator, where the sun is at an angle relative to the ground. Which compared to a solar panel with dual-axis sun tracking, they stated the tracking ones will only have 1.3x to 1.8x improvement. However, this is shown with comparison with a static panel with optimal orientation. Reading further into the study, the improvement for the tower (?, was not clear if they were referencing their tower or their cube design) was only 1.8x to 3x if comparing to the same testing condition as the tracking test.

In conclusion, the tower has only slightly better improvement in comparison to sun tracking solar panels and is only more noticeable at higher latitudes. However, they state that sun tracking is costly to implement and bulky and that the tower "can" be cheaper.

Honestly, whenever I hear of anything groundbreaking coming out of MIT, I take it with a fucking boulder of salt for exactly this reason.

I swear, sometimes it feels like they spend more money on their self-congratulatory PR office than actual research.
"slightly better"; is that what you call a 2 to 3 fold improvement?

When I wrote slight better, I was talking about when comparing to sun-tracking solar panels. Yes, 2 to 3 fold improvement is very good, whereas sun-tracking can only provide up to 2 times improvement.

I decided to re-analysis the study since this topic does interest me. I noticed when they are comparing the 3DPV (their towers) to a flat panel, they use "base area." I find this weird, why don't they use surface area of solar panels or similar? My conclusion is that they are talking about how much room the solar panels takes up on a flat surface. In other words, the 2 to 3 fold improvement is not in comparison to how much solar panel surface area is used but how much space they take up on a 2D plane, like a roof. This gives an advantage to the 3DPV since it takes up more volume but is not put into the equation.

Now, I can be wrong about their use of "base area", but for now, like /u/scorinth says, "take it with a fucking boulder of salt."
They basically stacked a bunch of solar panels on top of each other.

Article source is from 2012. Of the authors from the paper, only "Jeffrey C. Grossman" appears to have published after this paper. I have been unable to locate any further evidence that this "discovery" has been studied further, and there may be reasons its application is impracticable.
